title: HTTP Protocol
explanation: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the foundation of web communication. Clients send requests to servers, servers send responses. Each request has a method, headers, and optional body.
analogy: Like a formal letter exchange. You write a request letter (GET /menu), it includes your address (headers), and you receive a response letter with the requested information.
tiny_visual_key: client box sending arrow to server box, arrow back with response
example: GET /users/1 HTTP/1.1 requests user 1. Server responds with 200 OK and user data. POST /users with body creates a new user.
why_it_matters: Every web interaction uses HTTP. Understanding requests, responses, status codes, and headers is fundamental to building and debugging web applications.
checkpoint_question: What's the difference between GET and POST requests?
expected_answer: GET retrieves data and has no body - parameters go in the URL. POST sends data in the request body to create or modify resources. GET should be safe and idempotent.
common_mistake: Using GET for actions with side effects or sensitive data. GET requests are cached, bookmarked, and logged in browser history.
key_insight: HTTP is stateless - each request is independent. Cookies and sessions are workarounds to track state across requests.

title: HTTP Status Codes
explanation: Status codes are 3-digit numbers indicating request results. 2xx means success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client errors, 5xx server errors.
analogy: Like traffic lights with specific meanings. Green (200) means go ahead, yellow (3xx) means detour, red for you (4xx) means you messed up, red for system (5xx) means the road is broken.
tiny_visual_key: numbered categories: 2xx green, 3xx yellow, 4xx red, 5xx red
example: 200 OK (success), 201 Created (resource made), 301 Moved Permanently, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error.
why_it_matters: Status codes tell clients how to handle responses. APIs communicate success, errors, and next steps through these codes.
checkpoint_question: What's the difference between 401 and 403 status codes?
expected_answer: 401 Unauthorized means 'who are you?' - authentication is missing or invalid. 403 Forbidden means 'I know who you are, but you can't access this' - authenticated but not authorized.
common_mistake: Using 200 with an error message in the body. Status code should reflect the outcome - 400/500 for errors, not 200.
key_insight: The first digit tells the category: 2=success, 3=redirect, 4=your fault, 5=server's fault. This grouping helps quick debugging.

title: REST Architecture
explanation: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for web APIs. It uses HTTP methods on resources (nouns), is stateless, and returns representations of resources.
analogy: Like a library system. Books (resources) have locations (URLs). You can GET a book, POST to add one, PUT to replace, DELETE to remove. The library doesn't remember your last visit.
tiny_visual_key: resources as boxes, HTTP verbs as arrows acting on them
example: GET /users (list), GET /users/1 (read), POST /users (create), PUT /users/1 (replace), PATCH /users/1 (partial update), DELETE /users/1 (remove).
why_it_matters: REST is the dominant API style. Its conventions make APIs predictable - knowing REST means you can use any REST API immediately.
checkpoint_question: Why should REST APIs be stateless?
expected_answer: Each request contains all information needed to process it. This enables scalability (any server can handle any request), reliability (no state to lose), and caching.
common_mistake: Using verbs in URLs (POST /createUser) instead of nouns with HTTP methods (POST /users). REST is resource-oriented.
key_insight: REST maps CRUD operations to HTTP methods: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE. The URL is the resource, the method is the action.

title: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)
explanation: CORS is a security mechanism controlling which websites can access resources from another origin. Browsers block cross-origin requests by default; CORS headers allow exceptions.
analogy: Like a guest list at a private club. By default, only members (same origin) get in. The club can add guests to a list (CORS headers) to allow specific visitors.
tiny_visual_key: two origin boxes, browser blocking request unless CORS header allows
example: Site A (localhost:3000) calls API B (api.example.com). Browser sends preflight OPTIONS request. Server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * or specific origin.
why_it_matters: CORS errors are among the most common web development issues. Understanding CORS helps debug 'blocked by CORS policy' errors quickly.
checkpoint_question: Why do browsers enforce same-origin policy?
expected_answer: To prevent malicious scripts from accessing sensitive data across origins. Without it, evil-site.com could make requests to your-bank.com using your logged-in session.
common_mistake: Adding CORS headers in frontend code. CORS is enforced by browsers, configured on servers. The server must send the headers.
key_insight: CORS protects users, not servers. The server can always be called directly (curl ignores CORS). It prevents browser-based attacks.

title: HTML Document Structure
explanation: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) structures web content using nested elements. A document has a DOCTYPE, html root, head for metadata, and body for visible content.
analogy: Like a book's structure: DOCTYPE is the book type declaration, head is front matter (title, metadata), body is the content you read.
tiny_visual_key: nested boxes: DOCTYPE, html containing head and body
example:
Hello

Content
why_it_matters: HTML is the foundation of all web content. Correct structure ensures accessibility, SEO, and proper browser rendering.
checkpoint_question: What's the purpose of semantic HTML elements like <article>, <nav>, <main>?
expected_answer: They describe the meaning/role of content, not just appearance. This helps screen readers, search engines, and developers understand page structure.
common_mistake: Using divs for everything. Semantic elements (<header>, <section>, <footer>) improve accessibility and SEO without extra effort.
key_insight: HTML is about meaning, not appearance. A <button> isn't just styled differently - it has built-in keyboard handling, accessibility, and form behavior.

title: CSS Box Model
explanation: Every element is a box with four layers: content, padding (space inside border), border, and margin (space outside border). Width/height apply to the content by default.
analogy: Like a picture frame: the photo is content, matting is padding, the frame is border, and wall space between frames is margin.
tiny_visual_key: nested rectangles labeled margin, border, padding, content
example: With width:100px, padding:10px, border:5px, total rendered width is 130px (100 + 10*2 + 5*2) unless using box-sizing: border-box.
why_it_matters: Layout issues often stem from misunderstanding the box model. Knowing how size is calculated prevents 'why is this bigger than I specified?' confusion.
checkpoint_question: What does box-sizing: border-box change?
expected_answer: It includes padding and border in the element's specified width/height. A 100px element stays 100px regardless of padding/border, making sizing more intuitive.
common_mistake: Forgetting that margin doesn't affect element size but affects spacing. Two elements with 20px margins touch at 20px apart, not 40px (margin collapse).
key_insight: Always use box-sizing: border-box globally. It's how humans think about size and eliminates constant mental math.

title: CSS Flexbox
explanation: Flexbox is a 1D layout system for arranging items in rows or columns. The container controls direction, alignment, and distribution; items can flex to fill space.
analogy: Like arranging books on a shelf. You can center them, spread them evenly, push them to one end, or let some books take more space than others.
tiny_visual_key: container with items flexibly distributed along one axis
example: display: flex; justify-content: space-between puts first item at start, last at end, others evenly distributed.
why_it_matters: Flexbox solves alignment and distribution problems that were hacks in older CSS. Most UI layouts can be built with just flexbox.
checkpoint_question: What's the difference between justify-content and align-items?
expected_answer: justify-content aligns items along the main axis (horizontal in row, vertical in column). align-items aligns along the cross axis (perpendicular to main).
common_mistake: Confusing main and cross axis. The main axis follows flex-direction. justify is main axis, align is cross axis.
key_insight: Think of flexbox as: container sets the rules, items follow them. Most properties go on the container.

title: CSS Grid
explanation: CSS Grid is a 2D layout system for complex page layouts. You define rows and columns on a container, then place items into specific grid areas.
analogy: Like a spreadsheet. You define how many columns and rows, set their sizes, then place content in specific cells or spanning multiple cells.
tiny_visual_key: grid lines forming cells with items placed in specific areas
example: grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr creates 3 columns where the middle is twice as wide. grid-area places items in named regions.
why_it_matters: Grid handles 2D layouts that were impossible or hacky before. It's essential for page layouts, dashboards, and complex card arrangements.
checkpoint_question: When would you use Grid over Flexbox?
expected_answer: Grid for 2D layouts where you need control over both rows AND columns simultaneously. Flexbox for 1D layouts (items in a row OR column).
common_mistake: Using Grid for simple 1D layouts. Flexbox is simpler for centering or distributing items along one axis.
key_insight: Grid controls both dimensions from the container. Unlike flexbox, you can precisely place items without thinking about source order.

title: The DOM
explanation: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's tree representation of HTML. JavaScript uses the DOM to read and modify page content, structure, and styles dynamically.
analogy: HTML is the blueprint, DOM is the actual building. You can walk through rooms (traverse nodes), repaint walls (change styles), or add furniture (insert elements).
tiny_visual_key: tree structure with document at root, nodes branching down
example: document.getElementById('title').textContent = 'New Title' changes an element's text. document.createElement('div') creates a new element.
why_it_matters: All dynamic web behavior works through the DOM. Frameworks abstract it, but understanding the DOM helps debug issues and optimize performance.
checkpoint_question: Why can DOM manipulation be slow?
expected_answer: Each change can trigger browser recalculation of layout, styles, and repainting. Batch changes and minimize direct DOM access for better performance.
common_mistake: Selecting elements inside loops. Cache selections outside loops. Also, innerHTML for untrusted content creates XSS vulnerabilities.
key_insight: The DOM is live - changes are immediately reflected. But this power means careless updates cause performance issues.

title: Event Handling
explanation: Events are user or system actions (clicks, typing, page load). Event handlers are functions that run in response. Events bubble up from target to ancestors by default.
analogy: Like setting up a doorbell callback. When someone presses the button (event), your response (handler) is triggered. The sound can reach multiple rooms (bubbling).
tiny_visual_key: element with click arrow triggering handler function
example: button.addEventListener('click', () => alert('Clicked!')). Form submissions, key presses, mouse movement all trigger events.
why_it_matters: Events are how users interact with web apps. Understanding event handling, bubbling, and delegation is essential for interactive UIs.
checkpoint_question: What is event delegation and why use it?
expected_answer: Attach one handler to a parent instead of many handlers to children. Use event.target to identify which child triggered it. Better performance and works with dynamically added elements.
common_mistake: Adding handlers in loops without considering memory. If you add 1000 click handlers to 1000 items, consider one delegated handler on the parent.
key_insight: Events carry information: what happened, where, and context. The event object is your source of truth for handling user interaction.

title: Asynchronous JavaScript
explanation: JavaScript is single-threaded but non-blocking. Async operations (network requests, timers) don't block execution. Callbacks, Promises, and async/await handle async results.
analogy: Like ordering coffee. You don't stand frozen until it's ready - you take a number (callback/promise) and continue. When called, you get your coffee.
tiny_visual_key: main thread continuing while async operation processes separately
example: fetch() returns a Promise. You can .then() to handle the result or await it in an async function.
why_it_matters: Web apps are inherently async - network requests, user input, animations. Understanding async patterns prevents freezing UIs and callback hell.
checkpoint_question: What problem does async/await solve compared to .then() chains?
expected_answer: It makes async code look synchronous and linear. Instead of nested .then() chains, you write sequential code with await. Error handling uses regular try/catch.
common_mistake: Forgetting that async functions return Promises. If you call async function without await, you get a Promise, not the resolved value.
key_insight: async/await is syntax sugar over Promises. The code looks sync but isn't - other code runs while awaiting.

title: The Event Loop
explanation: The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model. It processes the call stack, then checks task queues for callbacks. Microtasks (Promises) run before macrotasks (setTimeout).
analogy: Like a chef with one hand. They can only do one thing at a time, but they have a priority list: finish current dish (stack), check VIP orders (microtasks), then regular orders (macrotasks).
tiny_visual_key: loop checking stack then microtask queue then macrotask queue
example: console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4); // Output: 1, 4, 3, 2
why_it_matters: Understanding the event loop explains timing mysteries - why setTimeouts don't run immediately, why Promises run before timeouts, why heavy code blocks the UI.
checkpoint_question: Why does a Promise callback run before a setTimeout(..., 0)?
expected_answer: Promises go to the microtask queue, setTimeout to the macrotask queue. The event loop processes all microtasks before any macrotasks after each stack clearance.
common_mistake: Assuming setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately. It queues for the next macrotask cycle - after the current code and all pending microtasks.
key_insight: JavaScript has one thread but multiple queues. Long-running code blocks everything - keep the stack clear for responsive UIs.

title: Component-Based Architecture
explanation: Modern frontends are built from reusable components - self-contained units of UI with their own state, logic, and rendering. Components compose into larger UIs.
analogy: Like LEGO blocks. Each block (component) is complete on its own. You combine blocks to build complex structures, and can reuse the same block type many times.
tiny_visual_key: nested component boxes combining into full page
example: A Button component used everywhere. A UserCard component that contains Avatar, Name, and ActionButtons components.
why_it_matters: Components enable reuse, isolation, and easier testing. Modern frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte) are all component-based.
checkpoint_question: What's the advantage of component isolation?
expected_answer: Changes to one component don't affect others. Bugs are contained, testing is focused, and teams can work on different components in parallel.
common_mistake: Making components too large or too small. A component should do one thing well. If it's hard to name, it might be too complex or too trivial.
key_insight: Think in components: what's the smallest useful UI piece? Build up from there. Components are the atoms of modern web UIs.

title: State Management
explanation: State is data that changes over time and affects rendering. Managing state means deciding where state lives, how it's updated, and how components access it.
analogy: Like the score in a game. Multiple displays might show it, various events can change it, but there's one source of truth. State management is tracking that score properly.
tiny_visual_key: central state box with arrows to multiple UI components
example: Local state (useState in React), lifted state (parent holds state for siblings), global state (Redux, Context, Zustand).
why_it_matters: Most bugs are state bugs. Proper state management prevents inconsistencies, makes debugging easier, and enables features like undo/redo and time-travel debugging.
checkpoint_question: When should you lift state up vs use global state?
expected_answer: Lift state when only a few nearby components need it - put it in their common ancestor. Use global state when many unrelated components need the same data.
common_mistake: Putting everything in global state. Start local, lift when needed. Global state adds complexity and re-renders.
key_insight: State flows down (props), events flow up (callbacks). This unidirectional flow makes data changes predictable.

title: Virtual DOM
explanation: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the real DOM. Frameworks compare new and old virtual DOMs (diffing), then apply minimal changes to the real DOM (reconciliation).
analogy: Like drafting a document. Instead of printing every edit, you make changes to a draft (virtual), compare with the current print (diff), and only reprint changed pages.
tiny_visual_key: virtual tree compared with previous, arrows to real DOM for changes
example: React renders to a virtual DOM, diffs against the previous render, and only updates changed elements in the real DOM.
why_it_matters: Direct DOM manipulation is slow. The virtual DOM batches changes and minimizes expensive real DOM operations, improving performance.
checkpoint_question: Why is diffing the virtual DOM faster than directly updating the DOM?
expected_answer: JavaScript object comparison is fast. Real DOM updates trigger layout, paint, and composite operations. Minimizing real DOM changes via diffing avoids these expensive operations.
common_mistake: Thinking virtual DOM means 'never touches real DOM'. It still updates the real DOM - just minimally. Also, not all frameworks use virtual DOM.
key_insight: Virtual DOM is a trade-off: extra memory and diffing time to reduce DOM manipulation. For most apps, it's a net win.

title: Server-Side Basics
explanation: Backend servers handle HTTP requests, run business logic, access databases, and return responses. They're the 'back' in frontend/backend - invisible to users but essential.
analogy: Like a kitchen in a restaurant. Customers (frontend) don't see it, but that's where orders are prepared, ingredients are managed, and recipes are followed.
tiny_visual_key: server box with database and business logic, connected to client
example: User clicks 'Buy'. Frontend sends POST /orders. Backend validates, charges payment, creates database record, returns confirmation.
why_it_matters: Most real apps need backends for data persistence, security, integration with external services, and logic that can't run in browsers.
checkpoint_question: Why run certain logic on the server instead of in the browser?
expected_answer: Security (secrets, validation), trust (users can modify client code), data access (databases), performance (heavy computation), and cross-client consistency.
common_mistake: Trusting client-side validation. Always validate on the server - client validation is for UX, server validation is for security.
key_insight: Clients ask, servers decide. Never trust client input - validate everything server-side.

title: Middleware
explanation: Middleware are functions that process requests between receiving them and sending responses. They can modify requests, validate, log, authenticate, or short-circuit with errors.
analogy: Like checkpoints before entering a venue. First security check (auth), then ticket scan (validation), then coat check (logging). Each step can allow, modify, or reject you.
tiny_visual_key: request passing through multiple function boxes before handler
example: Request → logger middleware → auth middleware → rate limiter → actual route handler → response
why_it_matters: Middleware enables clean separation of concerns. Auth, logging, validation, error handling can be reused across routes without duplicating code.
checkpoint_question: How does middleware allow or block request processing?
expected_answer: Middleware calls next() to pass to the next middleware or handler. If it doesn't call next() and sends a response instead (like 401 Unauthorized), processing stops.
common_mistake: Forgetting to call next() in middleware that should continue. The request hangs forever waiting for a response.
key_insight: Middleware is the request pipeline. Order matters - earlier middleware runs first and can affect or stop later processing.

title: Authentication vs Authorization
explanation: Authentication verifies identity (who are you?). Authorization determines permissions (what can you do?). Auth happens first, then authz checks if the authenticated user can perform the action.
analogy: Authentication is showing your ID at the door. Authorization is checking if you're on the VIP list for the VIP section. You can be authenticated but not authorized for everything.
tiny_visual_key: login check arrow to permission check arrow to resource
example: Login with username/password (authentication) succeeds. User tries to delete admin content - authz check fails, 403 Forbidden.
why_it_matters: Confusing these leads to security bugs. Every protected action needs both: verify identity, then verify permission for that specific action.
checkpoint_question: Why must authorization checks happen on every request, not just login?
expected_answer: Permissions can change after login, users might manipulate requests to access resources they shouldn't, and authentication alone doesn't prove permission for specific actions.
common_mistake: Checking permissions only on the frontend. Backend must verify authorization - frontend checks are for UX, not security.
key_insight: Authentication answers 'who are you?' Authorization answers 'can you do this?' Both are required for security.

title: Sessions and JWTs
explanation: Sessions store state server-side; client gets only a session ID cookie. JWTs are self-contained tokens with encoded claims - the client holds all auth data, signed by the server.
analogy: Sessions: valet parking where they keep your keys (state). JWT: carrying your own stamped ticket that proves you paid - everything's on the ticket.
tiny_visual_key: session: ID pointing to server storage; JWT: self-contained signed token
example: Session: Set-Cookie: sessionId=abc123. Server looks up abc123 in store. JWT: Authorization: Bearer eyJ... Server verifies signature, reads claims from token.
why_it_matters: Choosing session vs JWT affects architecture, scalability, and security. Sessions need shared storage for scaling; JWTs are stateless but have revocation challenges.
checkpoint_question: Why is revoking a JWT harder than revoking a session?
expected_answer: Sessions can be deleted from the server store immediately. JWTs are stateless - the server can't 'delete' them. You need blocklists or short expiration times.
common_mistake: Storing JWTs in localStorage (XSS vulnerable) or putting sensitive data in JWT payload (readable by anyone). Use httpOnly cookies and minimal claims.
key_insight: Sessions trade simplicity for server state. JWTs trade complexity (rotation, revocation) for statelessness. Neither is universally better.

title: SQL vs NoSQL
explanation: SQL databases are relational (tables, rows, schemas, joins). NoSQL covers non-relational stores (documents, key-value, graph, column). Each excels at different access patterns.
analogy: SQL is like a spreadsheet with strict columns and formulas linking sheets. NoSQL is like filing cabinets where each folder can have different contents - flexible but less structured.
tiny_visual_key: SQL: rigid table grid; NoSQL: flexible document shapes
example: SQL: PostgreSQL, MySQL - structured data, complex queries. NoSQL: MongoDB (documents), Redis (key-value), Neo4j (graph).
why_it_matters: Choosing the right database affects query capability, scalability, and development speed. Mismatches cause pain - relational data in NoSQL or flexible data forced into rigid schemas.
checkpoint_question: When is a document database better than a relational one?
expected_answer: When data is naturally hierarchical (nested objects), schemas vary per record, you need horizontal scaling, or you're doing simple key-based lookups without complex joins.
common_mistake: Choosing NoSQL because 'it scales better' without understanding your access patterns. SQL databases scale well for many use cases and offer consistency guarantees.
key_insight: Choose based on data relationships and access patterns. Complex relationships = SQL. Simple lookups or flexible documents = NoSQL.

title: Database Indexing
explanation: An index is a data structure that speeds up queries by avoiding full table scans. It's like a book index - look up a term to find the page directly instead of reading everything.
analogy: Like a phone book alphabetized by last name. Finding 'Smith' is fast - jump to S section. Without the index, you'd check every entry from A to Z.
tiny_visual_key: index tree pointing to row locations, skip scanning
example: CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email). Now 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ...' looks up the index instead of scanning all rows.
why_it_matters: Queries on unindexed columns scan entire tables - fine for 100 rows, disaster for 10 million. Proper indexing can turn minutes into milliseconds.
checkpoint_question: Why shouldn't you index every column?
expected_answer: Indexes cost storage space and slow down writes (every insert/update must update indexes). Index columns you query/filter by frequently, not everything.
common_mistake: Creating indexes after performance problems appear. Design indexes with your queries from the start. Also, compound indexes have column order that matters.
key_insight: Indexes trade write speed and storage for read speed. Profile your actual queries to know what to index.

title: ORMs and Query Builders
explanation: ORMs (Object-Relational Mappers) let you work with database records as programming objects. Query builders provide programmatic query construction. Both abstract raw SQL.
analogy: Like a translator. Instead of speaking SQL directly to the database, you describe what you want in your language (code), and the ORM translates to SQL.
tiny_visual_key: code objects with arrow through ORM to SQL and database
example: User.findById(1) instead of 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1'. User.create({name: 'Alice'}) instead of INSERT INTO...
why_it_matters: ORMs speed up development, reduce SQL injection risks, and provide type safety. But they can hide performance issues and generate suboptimal queries.
checkpoint_question: When should you bypass the ORM and write raw SQL?
expected_answer: For complex queries the ORM can't express efficiently, bulk operations, performance-critical paths, or database-specific features. Use EXPLAIN to verify ORM queries are efficient.
common_mistake: N+1 queries: fetching a list then querying related items one by one. ORMs make this easy to do accidentally. Use eager loading or joins.
key_insight: ORMs are productivity tools, not magic. Understand the SQL they generate, especially for performance-critical queries.

title: Web Performance Basics
explanation: Web performance is about speed: how fast content loads, renders, and becomes interactive. Key metrics include Time to First Byte, First Contentful Paint, and Time to Interactive.
analogy: Like judging a restaurant by wait times: how fast you're seated (TTFB), when appetizers arrive (FCP), and when you can fully enjoy your meal (TTI).
tiny_visual_key: timeline with TTFB, FCP, LCP, TTI markers
example: Core Web Vitals: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint < 2.5s), FID (First Input Delay < 100ms), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift < 0.1).
why_it_matters: Performance affects user experience, SEO rankings, and conversion rates. Every 100ms delay can reduce conversions. Google ranks based on Core Web Vitals.
checkpoint_question: What causes high Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)?
expected_answer: Images/embeds without size attributes, dynamically injected content above existing content, web fonts causing text reflow. Content shifts as things load, frustrating users.
common_mistake: Optimizing for the wrong metric. Measure first. A slow API might matter more than image compression. Focus on what actually impacts your users.
key_insight: Performance is perceived speed, not just technical speed. Skeleton loaders and progressive enhancement can make slow loads feel fast.

title: Caching Strategies
explanation: Caching stores computed results for reuse. Browser caching stores assets locally. Server caching stores computed responses. CDN caching distributes content geographically.
analogy: Like keeping frequently used items on your desk instead of walking to storage each time. The closer and more recently used, the faster to access.
tiny_visual_key: request checking cache layers: browser, CDN, server, database
example: Cache-Control: max-age=3600 tells browsers to cache for 1 hour. Redis stores database query results. CDN caches static assets worldwide.
why_it_matters: Caching dramatically reduces latency and server load. A cache hit can be 100x faster than computing the result. Most performance optimization is caching.
checkpoint_question: How do you force browsers to fetch new versions of cached files?
expected_answer: Cache-busting: include content hash in filename (app.abc123.js). When content changes, hash changes, URL changes, so browsers treat it as new. Or use Cache-Control headers strategically.
common_mistake: Caching user-specific data with shared keys, serving stale personalized content. Also, forgetting to invalidate caches when data changes.
key_insight: There are only two hard problems in CS: cache invalidation and naming things. Caching is powerful but requires careful invalidation strategy.

title: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
explanation: XSS injects malicious scripts into websites. If user input is rendered without escaping, attackers can run arbitrary JavaScript in victims' browsers, stealing sessions or data.
analogy: Like letting strangers write on your restaurant menu. If they write 'Free dessert!' customers get tricked. XSS lets attackers put their code on your site.
tiny_visual_key: malicious script in user input executing in victim browser
example: User submits '<script>stealCookies()</script>' as their name. If rendered raw in HTML, the script runs for everyone viewing that name.
why_it_matters: XSS is consistently in OWASP Top 10. A single XSS vulnerability can compromise all users, steal sessions, or deface your site.
checkpoint_question: Why isn't client-side input validation sufficient to prevent XSS?
expected_answer: Attackers can bypass the client entirely (curl, modified requests). Server must escape/sanitize output. Client validation is for UX, server validation is for security.
common_mistake: Using innerHTML or dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user content. Frameworks escape by default - don't bypass that protection.
key_insight: Never trust user input. Escape when outputting to HTML, not when storing. Use frameworks' auto-escaping and CSP headers as defense in depth.

title: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
explanation: CSRF tricks authenticated users into performing unwanted actions. If you're logged into your bank and visit a malicious site, it can submit forms to your bank using your session.
analogy: Like someone putting a 'transfer $1000' form in an email. When you open it (authenticated to your bank), clicking anything might submit the hidden transfer.
tiny_visual_key: evil site sending request to legitimate site using victim's session
example: Victim is logged into bank.com. Evil site has . Browser sends request with victim's bank cookies.
why_it_matters: CSRF can change passwords, transfer money, or modify data without the user's knowledge. Any state-changing action can be vulnerable.
checkpoint_question: How do CSRF tokens prevent this attack?
expected_answer: Server generates a unique token per session/form, embedded in legitimate forms. The token must be included in requests. Attackers can't read it from another origin, so they can't forge valid requests.
common_mistake: Only protecting POST requests. GET requests that change state are also vulnerable. Make GET requests safe (no side effects).
key_insight: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic cookie sending. Tokens prove the request came from your site, not a forged cross-site request.

title: SQL Injection
explanation: SQL injection inserts malicious SQL through user input. If queries concatenate user input without escaping, attackers can modify queries to bypass auth, extract data, or destroy tables.
analogy: Like a receptionist who types exactly what visitors say into the computer. If someone says 'Schedule meeting; also give me admin access', both commands run.
tiny_visual_key: user input with SQL escaping quotes, breaking intended query
example: Input: ' OR '1'='1. Query becomes: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='' OR '1'='1' - always true, returns all users.
why_it_matters: SQL injection can expose entire databases, bypass authentication, or destroy data. It's one of the oldest and most damaging vulnerabilities.
checkpoint_question: Why are parameterized queries safe against SQL injection?
expected_answer: Parameters are sent separately from the query. The database treats them as data, not code. Even if input contains SQL syntax, it's never executed as SQL.
common_mistake: Thinking escaping is enough. It helps but has edge cases. Always use parameterized queries/prepared statements - they're built into every database library.
key_insight: Never concatenate user input into SQL. Use parameterized queries everywhere. There are no exceptions to this rule.

title: CI/CD Pipelines
explanation: CI (Continuous Integration) automatically builds and tests code on every commit. CD (Continuous Deployment) automatically deploys passing builds. Together they enable rapid, safe releases.
analogy: Like an assembly line with quality checks. Every change triggers building (CI), testing (CI), and if it passes, shipping to customers (CD). Automation replaces manual steps.
tiny_visual_key: code commit triggering build, test, deploy steps
example: Push to main → GitHub Actions builds → runs tests → if pass, deploys to staging → manual approval → deploys to production.
why_it_matters: CI/CD catches bugs early, enables frequent releases, and reduces deployment risk. Manual deployments are error-prone and slow.
checkpoint_question: What's the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
expected_answer: Continuous Delivery: every commit is deployment-ready, but deployment requires manual approval. Continuous Deployment: every passing commit is automatically deployed to production.
common_mistake: Deploying without tests. CI without good test coverage just automates deploying bugs faster. Build testing into the pipeline.
code:
# GitHub Actions example
name: CI/CD
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
      - if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: ./deploy.sh
key_insight: CI/CD is about confidence. Automated tests give confidence to deploy frequently. Without tests, you're just deploying fear faster.

title: Environment Configuration
explanation: Applications need different settings per environment (dev, staging, prod). Configuration (database URLs, API keys) should be externalized, not hardcoded, typically via environment variables.
analogy: Like a restaurant with multiple locations. The recipes (code) are the same, but each location has different addresses, suppliers, and prices (configuration).
tiny_visual_key: same code box with different config boxes for each environment
example: DATABASE_URL differs between dev (localhost) and prod (managed database). API keys differ. Feature flags differ. Code stays the same.
why_it_matters: Hardcoded config causes bugs (wrong database in prod), security issues (secrets in code), and deployment friction. Externalized config enables consistent deployments.
checkpoint_question: Why should secrets never be in code repositories?
expected_answer: Repos are often shared, forked, or made public accidentally. Secrets in Git history are hard to remove. Use environment variables or secret managers.
common_mistake: Committing .env files with production secrets. Use .env.example with placeholder values. Real secrets go in CI/CD secrets or secret managers.
key_insight: Config is environment-specific; code is not. If it differs between environments, it's config. If it changes behavior everywhere, it's code.

title: Containers and Docker
explanation: Containers package an application with its dependencies into a portable unit. Docker creates containers from images - blueprints specifying OS, dependencies, and configuration.
analogy: Like shipping containers for code. Just as physical containers work on any ship, train, or truck, Docker containers run the same anywhere - your laptop, CI, or cloud.
tiny_visual_key: container box with app+dependencies, running on any host
example: Dockerfile defines: base image (node:18), copy code, install dependencies, specify run command. Build once, run anywhere.
why_it_matters: Containers eliminate 'works on my machine' problems. Development, CI, and production run identical environments. They enable microservices and cloud-native deployment.
checkpoint_question: How do containers differ from virtual machines?
expected_answer: VMs virtualize hardware and run full OS per VM. Containers share the host OS kernel, virtualizing only the app environment. Containers are lighter, faster to start, and more efficient.
common_mistake: Running as root in containers or including unnecessary files. Use non-root users, multi-stage builds, and .dockerignore for smaller, safer images.
code:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-slim
WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies first (layer caching)
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --production

# Copy source
COPY . .

# Non-root user
USER node

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
key_insight: Containers are about reproducibility. Same image = same behavior, whether locally, in CI, or across 1000 production instances.
